title: US and India Expand Defense and Civil Nuclear Ties Under Trump Administration
excerpt: A senior State Department official outlines plans to deepen cooperation in defense, nuclear energy, AI, and supply chains, as India's SHANTI Act clears the path for private-sector nuclear deals.
body:
• US Assistant Secretary of State S. Paul Kapur announced expanding defense and civil nuclear cooperation with India at a Hoover Institution roundtable attended by former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice.
  • India's SHANTI Act, enacted in late 2025, replaced the 1962 Atomic Energy Act and opened the nuclear sector to private players and up to 49% foreign direct investment, removing a key barrier to US-India nuclear commerce.
  • A delegation of senior US nuclear industry executives visited India earlier in 2026 to explore investment opportunities under the new liability framework.
  • India has acquired major US defense platforms over two decades, including Apache and Chinook helicopters, C-17 transport aircraft, P-8I patrol aircraft, and M777 howitzers.

The United States is expanding its defense partnership with India alongside deeper cooperation in civil nuclear energy, artificial intelligence, and emerging technologies, US Assistant Secretary of State for South and Central Asian Affairs S. Paul Kapur said in late July.

Speaking at a roundtable on India at Stanford's Hoover Institution — attended by former US Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice and former US Ambassador to India David C. Mulford — Kapur framed the deepening relationship as central to the Trump administration's Indo-Pacific strategy.

"Under this Administration, US engagement with India is creating jobs at home and strengthening supply chains that are critical to both the United States and the region."

— S. Paul Kapur, US Assistant Secretary of State

Defense Ties Accelerate

The remarks come as Washington and New Delhi continue to build on a framework for a major defense partnership signed in 2025, designed to strengthen interoperability across land, sea, air, space, and cyberspace.

India has significantly expanded its defense procurement from the United States over the past two decades. Major acquisitions include Boeing AH-64 Apache and CH-47 Chinook helicopters, C-17 Globemaster III and C-130J Super Hercules transport aircraft, P-8I Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft, and BAE Systems M777 ultra-light howitzers. In July 2026, Washington approved a $482.2 million military support deal covering India's Apache fleet and M777 systems.

Kapur indicated the next phase of cooperation would also focus on trusted AI adoption and other emerging technologies, reflecting broader efforts to build technology supply chains less dependent on China.

The SHANTI Act: A Nuclear Turning Point

The civil nuclear dimension of the relationship has been constrained for over a decade by India's liability laws. The Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act of 2010 gave operators the right to seek recourse against foreign suppliers in case of an accident — a provision that deterred US and European nuclear companies from entering the Indian market.

That changed with the enactment of the Sustainable Harnessing and Advancement of Nuclear Energy for Transforming India (SHANTI) Act, which replaced both the 1962 Atomic Energy Act and the 2010 liability law. The new legislation aligns India's nuclear liability framework with international standards, allows private-sector participation under regulatory oversight by the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board, and permits up to 49% foreign direct investment in select segments of the nuclear sector.

The US Embassy in India welcomed the law's passage, stating it was "a step towards a stronger energy security partnership and peaceful civil nuclear cooperation."

Industry Moves In

Earlier in 2026, Maria Korsnick, president and CEO of the Nuclear Energy Institute, led a 20-member delegation of US nuclear industry executives to India to explore commercial opportunities under the new framework.

"India has a very strong supply chain and very strong engineering talent. You're not new to nuclear. You understand it and have worked very well with it. That, to me, just makes the perfect partner."

— Maria Korsnick, President and CEO, Nuclear Energy Institute

The visit followed years of stalled commercial negotiations. Projects at Jaitapur in Maharashtra and Kovvada in Andhra Pradesh — designated for cooperation with France and the United States, respectively — had been delayed by liability concerns that the SHANTI Act now aims to resolve.

India's nuclear power capacity currently stands at 8,780 MW, with generation rising from 16,956 million units in 2007-08 to 56,681 million units in 2024-25. The government has set an ambitious target of 100 GW of nuclear capacity by 2047.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For Indian Americans in the energy and defense sectors, the expanding partnership represents concrete professional and business opportunities. The SHANTI Act's opening of India's nuclear market to private investment, combined with the US government's explicit support, creates a pathway for diaspora engineers, entrepreneurs, and investors with nuclear and defense industry expertise to participate in projects that were previously closed.

The broadening cooperation also has geopolitical implications. The explicit focus on supply-chain resilience and trusted AI adoption signals a deeper strategic alignment between Washington and New Delhi that extends well beyond traditional defense procurement — with implications for how the Indian-American community navigates its role in an evolving US-India relationship.
nri_angle: The expanding US-India defense and nuclear partnership, accelerated by the SHANTI Act, opens concrete opportunities for diaspora professionals in energy and defense while deepening strategic alignment between Washington and New Delhi.
